data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The single mechanism that best explains both the nocturnal UHI and its cross-city variance is the reduction in effective sky view factor (SVF), which traps daytime sensible heat by impeding longwave radiative cooling to the sky; cities with deeper, denser street canyons experience a more pronounced nighttime temperature gap.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a city has high thermal mass but completely flat, unobstructed terrain (SVF \u2248 1), the nocturnal UHI will be minimal regardless of heat storage.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If sustained nocturnal winds exceed 5 m/s, turbulent mixing will override radiative trapping and homogenize urban and rural temperatures.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If rural surroundings possess equally low sky view factors (e.g., dense forest canopy), the radiative cooling differential and UHI gap will vanish.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"After sunset, urban surfaces cool primarily by emitting longwave radiation to the cold sky. Deep street canyons and dense building arrays shrink the visible sky aperture (SVF), causing longwave radiation to bounce between opposing walls and be partially re-absorbed. This radiative trapping drastically lowers the net cooling rate of urban masonry and asphalt. Because daytime thermal mass storage is high, this trapped sensible heat is released slowly throughout the night, keeping the city air several degrees warmer. The cross-city variance scales directly with built density and building height, which dictate the SVF.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
